name: C#
title: C# from the first line
intro: C# (said "C sharp") is Microsoft's main language, released in 2000 with the .NET platform. It looks like Java and C++, but it has grown quickly: properties, LINQ queries, async code, records and pattern matching all arrived in C# before most of its neighbours. It runs Windows desktop programs, web services on any system, and games made with the Unity engine. Modern C# lets a program start straight away with top-level statements, without the class and Main wrapper older examples have. These lessons use C# 12 on .NET 8. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one yourself, install the .NET SDK, type dotnet new console -o hello, paste the example into hello/Program.cs and type dotnet run --project hello.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.summary: Top-level statements, Console.WriteLine and interpolated strings.

sections.p: A C# program can start with statements at the top of the file; the compiler wraps them in a Main method for you. Console.WriteLine prints a line and Console.Write prints without ending it. Statements end with a semicolon.

A string with a $ in front can hold expressions in braces, which are worked out and put in place. After a colon you can give a format: {price:F2} shows two decimals and {n,4} pads to four characters. A string with @ in front keeps backslashes as they are, which suits Windows paths.
sections.out:
Hazel has 7 nuts
14 after a good day
Cost: 1.50 [   7]
C:\Stash\nuts.txt

practice.why: Write doesn't end the line, so all three pieces land on one line.
Only the string with $ in front fills in the braces. The second is plain text.

lessons.title: Types and variables
lessons.summary: int, double, decimal, bool, string, var and null.

sections.p: Every variable has a type. int holds whole numbers, double numbers with a fraction, decimal exact decimal amounts such as money, bool true or false, char one character and string text. var lets the compiler take the type from the value. Dividing two ints drops the fraction. A double can't hold 0.1 exactly, which is why sums of money use decimal (numbers written with an m).

Strings have methods and properties: Length, ToUpper(), Contains, Replace, and [i] for one character counting from 0. In C#, == on strings compares the text, so it does what you would expect. Strings can't be changed; each method returns a new one.
sections.out:
12
SILVER BIRCH
S
True
Downy birch
True

sections.p: null means no object. With nullable checks turned on (the default in new projects), a string can't be null, but a string? can, and the compiler warns you before you use one without checking. ?. calls a method only if the value isn't null, and ?? gives a fallback.

practice.why: 7 / 2 is integer division. Once one side is a double, the result has a fraction. % is the remainder.
Index 1 is the second character. == compares the text of the two strings.

practice.q: Which type should hold a price like 19.99?
practice.why: decimal stores decimal fractions exactly. double and float use binary fractions, so 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.summary: if, switch expressions with patterns, for, foreach and while.

sections.p: if and else take a condition in brackets; && is and, || is or and ! is not. A switch expression picks a value by matching patterns: an exact value, a comparison like < 5, or several joined with and and or. _ matches anything else.
sections.out:
even dozen-ish
none, a few, plenty, a hoard

sections.p: for has a start, a test and a step. foreach visits every item in an array or list. while repeats as long as its condition holds. break leaves a loop and continue skips to the next pass.

practice.why: 10 falls in 9 to 11, 1 is listed with the winter months, and 5 matches only the _ case.
i is 0, 4 and 8, then 12 fails the test.

lessons.title: Methods and collections
lessons.summary: Methods, out and named arguments, List and Dictionary.

sections.p: A method has a return type, a name and typed parameters. In a program with top-level statements you can write methods right there, among the statements. Parameters can have default values, and callers can pass arguments by name. A method that has nothing to return uses void. A one-line method can use => instead of braces.

List<T> is a list that grows as you Add; Count gives its size and [i] reads by index. Dictionary<TKey, TValue> stores values under keys. TryGetValue looks a key up without failing when it is missing. A collection expression like [3, 1, 2] fills a collection in one go.

practice.code:
int Twice(int x) => x * 2;
Console.WriteLine(Twice(Twice(3)));
practice.why: The inner call gives 6 and the outer one doubles it again.
A List is an object. b = a copies the reference, so both names point at the same list.

lessons.title: Classes, records and interfaces
lessons.summary: Properties, constructors, records, interfaces and inheritance.

sections.p: A class describes a kind of object. C# uses properties, which look like fields from outside but can control who may change them: { get; private set; } can be read by anyone and changed only inside the class. A primary constructor, written in brackets after the class name, gives the class its constructor parameters directly.
A record is a type for plain data. One line gives you a constructor, read-only properties, equality that compares the values, and a readable ToString. with makes a copy with some values changed.

An interface lists members a type promises to have, and code can work with any type that implements it. A class can also inherit from one base class; an abstract member has no body in the base and must be supplied with override. The right version is chosen when the program runs.
sections.out:
chitter hoo chitter 
Owl says hoo

practice.why: with makes a new record and leaves p alone. The two now differ in Y, so == is False.

practice.q: What does { get; private set; } on a property mean?
options: Anyone can read it; only the class can change it
Anyone can change it; only the class can read it
It is a field, not a property
practice.answer: Anyone can read it; only the class can change it
practice.why: Each accessor can have its own access level. This is the usual way to keep an object in charge of its own data.

lessons.title: LINQ and async
lessons.summary: Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, and async methods with Task.

sections.p: LINQ (Language-Integrated Query) adds query methods to every collection. Where keeps items that pass a test, Select changes each item, OrderBy sorts, and Sum, Count and Max boil a sequence down to one value. The tests are lambdas, small functions written n => n * 2.

GroupBy collects items that share a key. Each group has a Key and can be counted or summed like any sequence. LINQ works the same way on lists in memory and, through libraries like Entity Framework, on database tables.
sections.out:
acorn: 2 stashes, 15 nuts
hazelnut: 1 stashes, 5 nuts

sections.p: An async method returns a Task, or Task<T> when it produces a value. await waits for a task without blocking the thread, which keeps apps responsive while they wait for files or the network. Task.WhenAll waits for several at once. Top-level statements may use await directly.

practice.why: oak, ash and elm have three letters, and beech is the first that starts with b.

practice.code:
var evens = Enumerable.Range(1, 6).Where(n => n % 2 == 0).Select(n => n * n);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join("+", evens) + "=" + evens.Sum());
practice.why: Range(1, 6) is 1 to 6. The even ones are 2, 4 and 6, and their squares add to 56.

lessons.title: Value types and reference types
lessons.summary: struct versus class, and what = really copies.

sections.p: C# has two kinds of types. A value type (int, double, bool and any struct) holds its data directly, so = copies the data. A reference type (any class, arrays, string) is reached through a reference, so = copies the reference and both names then point at the same object.

Arguments are copied in the same way. A method that gets a class object can change that object, but giving its parameter a new object does not affect the caller. Marking a parameter ref passes the caller's variable itself, so even a value type can be changed.
== on two class objects asks whether they are the same object. Records, structs and strings compare their contents instead. That is a good reason to use a record for plain data.

practice.why: List is a class, so a and b refer to the same list.
Pair is a struct, so y is an independent copy.

practice.q: What does ref on a parameter do?
options: Passes the caller's variable itself, so the method can change it
Turns a struct into a class
practice.answer: Passes the caller's variable itself, so the method can change it
practice.why: Without ref the method gets a copy of the value (or of the reference).

lessons.title: Exceptions and null safety
lessons.summary: try, catch, using, and the ?. and ?? operators.

sections.p: When something goes wrong, .NET throws an exception, and it travels up through the callers until a catch handles it. Catch the specific type you expect, such as FormatException from int.Parse. A finally block runs whether or not anything was thrown. For input that is often bad, int.TryParse avoids exceptions altogether.
sections.out:
got 12
checked
'twelve' is not a number
checked
14

sections.p: throw starts an exception. Pick a standard type that fits (ArgumentException for a bad argument, InvalidOperationException when the object is in the wrong state) and give a clear message. A when clause lets a catch handle only some cases.
sections.out:
refused: only 5 nuts stored
cannot add a negative number

sections.p: Objects that hold something outside .NET's memory, such as an open file or a network connection, implement IDisposable. A using declaration calls Dispose when the variable goes out of scope, even if an exception is thrown, so the resource is always released.
sections.out:
nuts.log: buried 3
nuts.log closed
caught owl!

sections.p: Modern C# projects turn on nullable reference types: string means never null, and string? means it may be null, and the compiler warns when you use a maybe-null value without checking. ?. reads a member only if the value is not null, giving null otherwise, and ?? supplies a fallback.

practice.why: The catch prints the message, finally always runs, and the program then carries on.
name?.Length is null because name is null, and ?? replaces it with 0.

practice.q: Why use int.TryParse instead of int.Parse for user input?
options: It reports failure with a bool instead of throwing
It is the only one that handles negative numbers
practice.answer: It reports failure with a bool instead of throwing
practice.why: Bad input is expected, not exceptional, so checking a bool is simpler and cheaper.

lessons.title: Generics, delegates and lambdas
lessons.summary: Code that works for many types, and functions as values.

sections.p: A generic type or method has a type parameter, written in angle brackets, that is filled in when it is used. List<T> is one. You can write your own, and a constraint such as where T : IComparable<T> says what the type must be able to do.

A delegate is a value that holds a method. The built-in Func<int, int> takes an int and returns one; Action<string> takes a string and returns nothing. A lambda such as n => n * 2 writes the method in place. Lambdas can use variables from around them, which is called capturing.

An event is a list of delegates that a class calls when something happens. Other code subscribes with +=. This is how buttons in a user interface tell your code they were clicked. ?.Invoke calls the event only if someone subscribed.
sections.out:
2 seeds left
0 seeds left
refill the feeder
squirrels are sad

practice.why: inc(3) is 4, and sq(4) is 16.
Lambdas capture the variable itself, not its value at the time, so both see x = 2 when they run.

practice.q: What does where T : IComparable<T> allow inside a generic method?
options: Calling CompareTo on values of type T
Creating new T objects with new T()
practice.answer: Calling CompareTo on values of type T
practice.why: The constraint promises every T has that method, so the compiler lets you call it.

lessons.title: Iterators and lazy sequences
lessons.summary: IEnumerable, yield return and deferred LINQ.

sections.p: foreach works on anything that is IEnumerable<T>. The easiest way to make one is a method with yield return: each time the loop asks for the next item, the method runs until the next yield return and then pauses there. Items are made only when needed, so a sequence can even be endless.

Most LINQ methods (Where, Select, Take) do not run when you call them. They build a recipe that runs when you loop over it. So the query below reads the list as it is when it is used, and the printing shows the steps happen one item at a time. ToList() runs the recipe immediately and keeps the results.
sections.out:
before the loop
  checking 4
big: 4
  checking 9
big: 9
  checking 2
  checking 12
big: 12
3

practice.why: Take(3) stops asking after three items, so the endless method only runs that far.
The query runs when Count() is called, after 3 was added.

options: The method hands back one item and pauses until the next is asked for
All items are produced at once
practice.answer: The method hands back one item and pauses until the next is asked for
practice.why: That is what makes iterators lazy, and why endless sequences work with Take.

lessons.title: Project: a nut inventory
lessons.summary: Records, LINQ, pattern matching and formatting together.

sections.p: This program keeps a small inventory of stores, each with nuts of different kinds and ages. It uses a record for the data, LINQ to group and total, a switch expression with patterns to label freshness, and format specifiers such as {name,-8} (left-aligned in 8 columns) and {n,4} (right-aligned in 4) to print a tidy table.
sections.out:
tree     nuts  freshest
oak        20  fresh
beech      20  fresh
hazel      13  fine
all        53
eat soon: acorn at the oak, hazelnut at the hazel

sections.p: Add a method that moves nuts from one store to another and throws if there are not enough, read the caches from a CSV file with File.ReadLines and Split(','), or make Freshness depend on the kind of nut as well, using a tuple pattern such as ("acorn", < 60).

practice.code: Console.WriteLine($"[{"ab",-4}][{7,3}]");
practice.why: A negative width left-aligns, a positive one right-aligns.
The arms are tried from the top; _ catches everything left.

practice.q: What does GroupBy(c => c.Tree) give you?
options: One group per tree, each with a Key and the caches for that tree
Only the first cache of each tree
practice.answer: One group per tree, each with a Key and the caches for that tree
practice.why: Each group can be totalled or searched with LINQ, as the program does with Sum and Min.
